patent: Filed 1966-11-14 and issued 1970-01-06 to Robert W. Chang and assigned to Bell Telephone Laboratories. It is Chang's patent on orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM). N data channels sit on carriers spaced f_{s} apart. Each channel is 2f_{s} wide and carries 2f_{s} bauds, so each spectrum overlaps its neighbours' by half. There are no guard bands, yet no intersymbol or interchannel interference, because the transmitting filters obey stated symmetries in amplitude and phase. The total rate is 2N/(N+1) bauds per cycle of bandwidth, approaching the Nyquist limit of 2 as N grows. The patent omits the proofs and refers to Chang, "Synthesis of Band-Limited Orthogonal Signals for Multichannel Data Transmission", Bell System Technical Journal, December 1966. The apparatus here is analog: shaping filters, mixers and tapped-delay-line matched filters (FIGS. 4 and 6). S. B. Weinstein and P. M. Ebert (IEEE Transactions on Communication Technology, 1971) showed that OFDM modulation and demodulation can be done with the discrete Fourier transform, the route later used in practice. OFDM now underlies ADSL (as discrete multitone), DAB and DVB-T broadcasting, Wi-Fi from IEEE 802.11a on, and the LTE and 5G NR cellular standards.

figs.1: General model of the system, with each block labelled by its impulse response. Impulses on lines 10-12 drive transmitting filters a_{1}(t) to a_{n}(t), whose passbands are centred f_{s} apart. Line 13 and the dashed connection stand for the channels that are not drawn. The outputs are summed onto line 14 and pass through a medium with impulse response h(t). Noise is added at 19. Receiver 20 is shown only as a box here; FIG. 6 gives a concrete receiver.
figs.2A: Shaping function 21, Q_{i}(f) = 1/2 cos 2π(f - f_{i})/2f_{s}, drawn from f_{i} - f_{s} to f_{i} + f_{s}. This span is one full cosine period: +1/2 at the channel centre, zero at f_{i} ± f_{s}/2 and -1/2 at the band edges. It is even about f_{i} and odd about f_{i} ± f_{s}/2, which are the two symmetries the theorem requires. The horizontal line is the zero level. C_{i} = 1/2 is the offset added in (B).
figs.2B: Curve (A) raised by C_{i} = 1/2 so that it reaches zero at the band edges. Raised cosine 22 = 1/2 + 1/2 cos 2π(f - f_{i})/2f_{s} is the required squared amplitude of the filter and medium together.
figs.2C: Square root of (B): curve 23 = cos π(f - f_{i})/2f_{s}, the positive half-cycle of a cosine. This is the amplitude response A_{i}(f)H(f) that the filter and medium must have together. Its full width of 2f_{s} is twice the channel spacing, so adjacent channels overlap by half.
figs.3A: A second shaping function 31 with a flat top, like the response of a multiple-tuned circuit. Its symmetries are the same as in FIG. 2(A): even about f_{i}, and odd about f_{i} ± f_{s}/2, where it crosses the zero line. The small ripples outside the main lobe near f_{i} ± f_{s} are part of the drawn response.
figs.3B: Curve 32 has the same shape as 31, with the ordinate shifted so that its minimum is zero; it is the squared amplitude response for this example. Its two maxima sit symmetrically about f_{i}, so the channel centre need not be where the response peaks.
figs.3C: Curve 33 is the square root of 32, the corresponding amplitude response A_{i}(f)H(f). Compared with the half-cosine of FIG. 2(C), it has a flatter top and steeper skirts.
figs.4: Three-channel transmitter built from one filter design. Data a, b and c arrive on lines 41-43. Each passes through an identical bandpass filter 44, which has response H_{1}(f), is 2f_{s} wide and is centred at (k + 0.5)f_{s}, k odd, outside the band of the medium. Modulators 45 mix with carriers f_{1} = (k-1)f_{s}, f_{2} = (k-2)f_{s} and f_{3} = (k-3)f_{s}, so the lower sidebands land at 1.5f_{s}, 2.5f_{s} and 3.5f_{s}. These are summed on line 46. Adder 47 adds a tone at f_{s}, for the receiver's timing and carriers. Low-pass filter 48 (H_{2}(f)) removes the upper sidebands, and modulator 50 with carrier f_{c} moves the composite signal into the passband of the medium on line 49.
figs.5: Spectra for FIG. 4, with frequency on the horizontal axis; it is not to scale between the left and right groups of curves. In rows (A)-(C), the right-hand group is the common filter: amplitude H_{1}(f) (solid half-cosines 55, 57, 59) and phase α_{1}(f) (dashed 56, 58, 60). The phase is a falling trend with a sinusoidal ripple and crosses the axis at the filter centre. Vertical line 61 in row (D) marks that centre, (k + 0.5)f_{s}. The left-hand curves are the lower sidebands that the three modulators produce: 51 at 1.5f_{s}, 52 at 2.5f_{s} and 53 at 3.5f_{s}. Row (D) shows them combined: each band edge falls on the neighbouring channel's peak, and the double arrow marks the spacing f_{s}. Curve 62 is the low-pass response H_{2}(f), flat to 4.5f_{s}. The unnumbered vertical line at f_{s} sits at the frequency of the tone added by adder 47.
figs.6: Receiver for the signal of FIG. 4; it is printed sideways on the sheet. The received signal arrives on line 65. Pick-off 70 extracts the f_{s} tone and derives from it the 2f_{s} sampling clock and the demodulating carriers, which go out on conductor 66. Line 73 feeds three branches. In each branch, modulator 74, with carrier f_{c}, f_{c} + f_{s} or f_{c} + 5f_{s}, moves one channel to 1.5f_{s}. Low-pass filter 76 (response 75, flat to 2.5f_{s}) then suppresses the channel that does not overlap it. Next come matched filter 78, which acts as a correlator, and sampler 79 at 2f_{s}; the output appears on lead 80, 81 or 82. Insets 83-85 show the three channels, as curves numbered 1-3, after filter 76. In the bottom branch the order is reversed, because the carrier f_{c} + 5f_{s} lies above the band.

parts.44: All three filters are the same. Each is centred at (k + 0.5)f_{s}, outside the band of the medium, and the modulators 45 move their outputs to the channel frequencies.
parts.47: Adds a component at f_{s}, from which the receiver derives its carriers and its sampling frequency.
parts.56: The phase α_{1}(f) of filters 44. Adjacent channels differ by 90 degrees plus an arbitrary phase function that is odd about the midpoint between their centres.
parts.61: Marks the centre frequency (k + 0.5)f_{s} of filters 44, not a signal.
parts.73: Not named in the text. In FIG. 6 it labels the common line that distributes the received signal to modulators 74.
parts.78: The text describes a tapped delay line whose tap weights are set from a test transmission, with taps spaced 1/6f_{s}. Its output is read at the time of peak response, when the adjacent orthogonal channel contributes zero.
parts.83: The numbers 1, 2 and 3 on the curves in insets 83-85 are channel numbers, not reference numerals.

glossary.def: Two signals are orthogonal when the time average of their product over a common interval is zero. A correlator matched to one of them then gives no output for the other, even when their spectra overlap.
Orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing: many low-rate data streams on closely spaced, overlapping subcarriers that are kept orthogonal so that they do not interfere.
Overlap in time between successive symbols on one channel, caused by band limiting and the spread of the channel impulse response.
Leakage of one frequency channel into the detector of another.
Unused spectrum (or time) left between channels so that they do not interfere; this patent removes it.
Symbols per second. A symbol may carry more than one bit; the patent allows m-ary symbols and analog samples.
At most 2W independent samples per second can be sent through bandwidth W without intersymbol interference: 2 bauds per cycle of bandwidth.
A spectrum shaped as 1/2 + 1/2 cos, which rolls off smoothly to zero; it is a standard pulse-shaping response.

Even: the function's mirror image about a point is the function itself. Odd: the mirror image is its negative. The product of two even or two odd functions is even; the product of an even and an odd function is odd.
The magnitude and phase angle of a filter's or medium's transfer function as functions of frequency, written here A_{i}(f), α_{i}(f) for filter i and H(f), η(f) for the medium.
Here a mixer: it multiplies a signal by a carrier, producing upper and lower sidebands, and so shifts the spectrum in frequency. At the receiver the same operation demodulates.
The difference-frequency copy of the spectrum produced by mixing; it is mirror-reversed in frequency.
The frequency range near zero, before translation to a carrier.
A filter whose impulse response is the time reverse of the expected signal. Its output, sampled at the peak, is the correlation of the input with that signal.
A delay line with outputs at equal intervals; weighting and summing the tap outputs forms a programmable filter (a transversal filter).
Random noise with a normal amplitude distribution, the standard model for thermal noise on a channel.
